Stronger
STRONG-er
adj. (comparative)
The comparative of strong, Saxon strang. Webster 1828: having more strength or power. Scripture uses it in comparisons that overturn the expected order — the weakness of God stronger than men, a prophet overpowered by the God he served.

Biblical Definition

Stronger in Scripture is nearly always used to overturn an expectation. Paul’s statement is the boldest: Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25). There is no foolishness in God and no weakness in Him; Paul is speaking of the cross as the world judges it, and saying that what men take for God’s weakest act outmatches their strongest. Jeremiah uses the word in a complaint that is also a confession: O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me (Jeremiah 20:7). He had resolved to stop preaching, and could not, because the word was as a burning fire shut up in my bones. Christ uses it of Himself in the parable of the strong man: when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils (Luke 11:22). And the chronicler measures a long conflict in one sentence: David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker (2 Samuel 3:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives STRONGER as the comparative of STRONG: having more physical or moral power; more able to sustain or resist; more forcible or cogent, as an argument.

expand to see more

STRONGER, a. — The comparative of STRONG; having greater power or force than another.

STRONG, a. — Having physical active power, or great power of acting; vigorous; able to sustain or resist.

Having moral or intellectual force; cogent; as, a strong argument or a strong reason.

Fortified; able to resist attack; as, a strong city or a strong hold.

From Saxon strang, strong — the root also of strength, string, and strain.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 1:25 — "Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men."

Jeremiah 20:7 — "O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me."

Luke 11:22 — "But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils."

2 Samuel 3:1 — "Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker."

Modern Corruption

Luke 11:22 pictures Satan as a strong man already overcome, disarmed and plundered by a stronger, which contradicts the popular Christianity that treats the devil as an active rival whose defeat still hangs on the believer’s technique.

expand to see more

The parable is the Lord’s own answer to the charge that He cast out devils by Beelzebub. A strong man armed keeps his palace and his goods are in peace — that is the world under the god of this world — but when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils. Each exorcism is a piece of plunder carried out of a house already entered. Colossians 2:15 says Christ spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it — at the cross, in the past tense. The believer’s warfare is real and Ephesians 6 arms him for it, but he fights from a victory, not toward one, and Scripture nowhere makes the outcome depend on the right formula spoken with sufficient authority.

Jeremiah 20:7 is worth defending because it embarrasses modern readers in both directions. The prophet says God deceived him — the Hebrew is a strong word, used elsewhere of enticing — and says that God was stronger and prevailed. He is not accusing God of falsehood; he is saying he was overpowered into an office that has cost him everything and that he cannot lay down. Scripture records the complaint without correcting it, and two verses later Jeremiah says he resolved to speak no more in God’s name and found he could not forbear. A canon that includes this is a canon that does not require the sufferer to be composed, and 1 Corinthians 1:25 explains why the whole pattern holds: God’s apparent weakness is stronger than men’s strength.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ischuros (G2478), strong; ischuroteros, stronger; asthenes (G772), weak; Hebrew chazaq (H2388), strong, firm; pathah (H6601), to entice, to persuade.

expand to see more

Greek ischuroteros — comparative of ischuros (G2478); the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25).

Greek asthenes (G772) — without strength, weak; the term Paul deliberately applies to God’s act at the cross as men judge it.

Greek panoplia (G3833) — full armour; the strong man’s armour taken in Luke 11:22, and the believer’s in Ephesians 6:11.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to prevail; thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed (Jeremiah 20:7).

Hebrew pathah (H6601) — to entice, to persuade, to open; the verb the KJV renders deceived in the same verse.

Usage

"The weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25) — the cross as the world judges it, outmatching man’s best."

"Thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed (Jeremiah 20:7) — a prophet overpowered into an office he cannot lay down."

"When a stronger than he shall come upon him (Luke 11:22) — the strong man already entered, disarmed, and plundered."
